metal.notes: Aluminium cans in the 150 ml to 3 L range are worth 10 cents each under the Victorian CDS, and refund points accept them by the bagful — a household's cans add up faster than most people expect.
metal.dropOff: CDS Vic refund points for eligible cans; council transfer station or a scrap metal yard for pots, pans and larger metal.

organic.disposal: Put all food scraps and garden waste in the green-lid FOGO bin, collected weekly.
prepSteps: Use the kitchen caddy with newspaper or an AS 4736 certified compostable liner
Include meat, bones, dairy and citrus — commercial composting handles them all
Empty the caddy into the green bin every day or two in summer
Keep branches under the length your council specifies, and leave soil and rocks out
acceptedExamples: Soiled paper towel and shredded paper, where the council allows it
rejectedExamples: Plastic bags, including 'degradable' ones (they shred into the compost and fail the AS 4454 standard)
Compostable coffee cups and cutlery that are not AS 4736 certified (they do not break down in the process time)
Dog waste and kitty litter unless your council explicitly allows it (pathogen limits)
Treated timber and painted wood (preservative chemicals end up in farm compost)
Soil, rocks and rubble (heavy, abrasive and of no compost value)
organic.notes: FOGO compost goes to Victorian farms and landscape supplies, and that end market is why the standard is so strict about plastic: contamination above a low threshold sends a whole load to landfill. Every Victorian council is required to offer a FOGO service by 2027.
organic.dropOff: Large garden loads: council green waste drop-off at the transfer station, often free for a set number of visits per year.

ewaste.disposal: Take e-waste to a council transfer station, a resource recovery centre or a retailer drop-off — it is banned from all kerbside bins in Victoria.
prepSteps: Back up and factory-reset the device, then remove SIM and memory cards
Remove loose batteries and hand them in separately
Bring the cables and charger with the device
Check your council's website: many offer free e-waste drop-off and some collect it at the kerb on request
acceptedExamples: Power tools and their battery packs
rejectedExamples: Any e-waste in the red bin (banned from Victorian landfill since 1 July 2019)
E-waste in the yellow bin (it is not packaging and damages the sorting plant)
Vapes in any kerbside bin (lithium batteries — a documented cause of truck fires)
Fridges and air conditioners left on the nature strip (refrigerant must be degassed by a licensed operator)
ewaste.notes: The Victorian e-waste landfill ban is enforced statewide and every council has a drop-off point within reach, while Officeworks, Battery World and the National Television and Computer Recycling Scheme cover most small items for free.
ewaste.dropOff: Council transfer station or resource recovery centre, Officeworks and retailer drop-off boxes, and B-cycle battery collection points.

hazardous.disposal: Take household chemicals to a free Detox Your Home event or a permanent drop-off site — never any kerbside bin.
prepSteps: Keep everything in its original labelled container
Never mix chemicals, and do not decant into food or drink containers
Tape the terminals of lithium and button batteries before transport
Book a Detox Your Home session if your nearest site requires it, and check the 20 kg or 20 L limit
acceptedExamples: Motor oil, coolant and brake fluid
Fluorescent tubes and compact fluorescent globes
rejectedExamples: Batteries in any kerbside bin (they have caused fires in Melbourne trucks and at sorting facilities)
Paint tipped down the stormwater drain (it flows untreated into the Yarra and Port Phillip Bay)
Medicines in the bin or toilet (return them to a pharmacy under the RUM project)
Half-full aerosols in the yellow bin (only genuinely empty cans belong there)
Asbestos taken to a general transfer station (it needs a licensed facility and prior arrangement)
hazardous.notes: Detox Your Home is a free Sustainability Victoria service and includes a permanent network of drop-off sites as well as mobile events, and B-cycle battery drop-off points are now in most supermarkets and hardware stores. Paint is also covered by Paintback at participating sites.
hazardous.dropOff: Detox Your Home events and permanent sites, Paintback drop-offs, B-cycle battery points, and pharmacies for medicines through the Return Unwanted Medicines project.

textile.binName: Op shop or textile recovery point
textile.disposal: Take clean, dry clothing to an op shop during opening hours or to a charity clothing bin.
prepSteps: Wash and dry everything before donating
Donate inside the shop during opening hours — bags left at a closed door are illegal dumping and cost charities millions each year
Tie shoes together in pairs
Separate genuinely unwearable fabric for a textile recovery bin rather than an op shop
rejectedExamples: Textiles in the yellow recycling bin (fabric wraps around the sorting equipment)
Wet or mouldy clothing (it ruins everything packed with it)
Bags left outside a closed op shop (rain and scavenging turn a donation into landfill)
Oily rags and paint-soaked cloth (fire risk — Detox Your Home)
Broken, stained items handed to a charity shop (charities pay to send unsellable donations to landfill)
textile.notes: Australia sends a very large volume of clothing to landfill per person, and op shops carry the disposal cost of unsellable donations, so honest sorting matters: sellable items to the shop, worn-out fabric to a dedicated textile recovery bin like Upparel or a council textile collection.
textile.dropOff: Charity op shops, charity clothing bins, retailer take-back programs, and council textile recovery collections.

trash.disposal: Bag it and put it in the red-lid rubbish bin.
prepSteps: Bag waste so nothing escapes when the truck tips the bin
Wrap broken glass and sharps in newspaper and label the bundle
Keep the lid closed and the bin under its weight limit or it will not be collected
Put the bin out with the lid arrows facing the road for the automated arm
acceptedExamples: Soft plastics such as bread bags, chip packets and cling wrap
Disposable coffee cups without a compostable certification
rejectedExamples: E-waste of any kind (banned from Victorian landfill)
Batteries and vapes (fire risk — B-cycle drop-off instead)
Food and garden waste (FOGO takes both, and green bin capacity is free)
Hot ashes from a barbecue or fireplace (they have set alight bins and trucks)
Building rubble and soil (weight limit; take it to the transfer station)
trash.notes: Victoria's landfill levy makes the red bin the most expensive stream for your council, and with FOGO and the purple glass bin running, a well-sorted household usually finds the red bin is the emptiest of the four.
trash.dropOff: Hard rubbish: your council's annual or on-request hard waste collection, or the transfer station.

regions.name: Toronto — Blue Bin, Green Bin and Garbage
regions.authority: City of Toronto Solid Waste Management Services
regions.notes: Toronto runs three carts — Blue Bin recycling, Green Bin organics and a grey Garbage bin — with the Green Bin collected weekly and the other two on alternating weeks. Two things make it unusual: the Green Bin uses anaerobic digestion, so it takes diapers, pet waste and even plastic bag liners that almost no other city will accept, and the garbage bin is charged by size, so shrinking it saves real money. The mistake that fills the city's contamination reports is the black plastic takeout container, which the optical sorters at the recycling facility physically cannot see and which therefore belongs in the garbage.

bins.name: Blue Bin (recycling)
bins.description: Every-other-week recycling cart for containers, paper and cardboard, placed loose. Clean plastic film is the one exception: bundle it inside a single tied bag.

bins.name: Green Bin (organics)
bins.description: Weekly organics cart processed by anaerobic digestion at the Dufferin and Disco facilities, producing biogas and digestate.

bins.name: Garbage Bin
bins.description: Every-other-week garbage cart in four sizes, from small to extra-large, with the annual fee rising with the size you choose.

bins.name: Drop-off Depot / Community Environment Day
bins.description: The City's Drop-off Depots and Household Hazardous Waste depots take electronics and chemicals free of charge; the Toxic Taxi collects larger quantities from your door.

bins.name: Textile drop box or charity donation
bins.description: Charity donation bins and textile drop boxes, including the containers at City Drop-off Depots run with charity partners.

plastic.disposal: Empty and rinse plastic containers and put them loose in the Blue Bin; bundle clean film inside one tied bag.
prepSteps: Rinse out food and drink residue
Put the lid back on bottles and jugs so it is not lost through the screens
Collect clean plastic bags, overwrap and film in one bag, tie it shut and put that in the bin
Keep black plastic out — it goes in the garbage
acceptedExamples: Yogurt, margarine and sour cream tubs
Clear clamshell containers for berries and salads
Plastic bags, bread bags and overwrap, bagged together
Plastic lids from paper coffee cups
rejectedExamples: Black plastic takeout containers and trays (optical sorters cannot detect carbon black, so they end up as residue)
Compostable and biodegradable plastics (they look like PET to the sorter and are not accepted in the Green Bin either)
Polystyrene foam containers and packing peanuts (Toronto removed foam from the Blue Bin list)
Plastic toys, hangers and hoses (not packaging — they jam the sorting line)
Containers that held motor oil or chemicals (hazardous residue — HHW depot)
plastic.notes: Toronto is one of the few large North American programs that takes plastic film at the kerb, but only bagged together — loose bags shut the sorting line down. Ontario's Blue Box program moved to full producer responsibility in 2023 and 2026, so the accepted-materials list is now set province-wide rather than by the City alone.
plastic.dropOff: Foam and film in quantity: City Drop-off Depots; the Waste Wizard search tool settles any doubtful item.

paper.disposal: Put clean, dry paper loose in the Blue Bin.
prepSteps: Keep paper dry — Blue Bin collection is only every other week
Leave staples and window envelopes in place
Bag shredded paper in a clear or paper bag so it does not blow away
Put soiled paper towel and napkins in the Green Bin instead
acceptedExamples: Paper coffee cups, with the lid recycled separately
Paper bags and gift wrap without foil
rejectedExamples: Thermal-paper receipts (the coating contaminates recycled pulp)
Tissues, paper towel and napkins (Green Bin — they are organics in Toronto)
Foil-lined and glittered wrapping paper (the metallised layer is not fibre)
Photographs and laminated sheets (plastic layers)
Wet or greasy paper (moisture and oil ruin the bale)
paper.notes: Toronto accepts paper hot-drink cups in the Blue Bin, which is unusual in North America, but the lid must be separated and the cup emptied — a cup with coffee still in it soaks the paper around it.
paper.dropOff: Shredded paper in bulk and surplus cardboard: City Drop-off Depots.

cardboard.disposal: Flatten boxes and put them in the Blue Bin, or beside it if they are bundled and tied.
prepSteps: Remove tape, labels and any foam or plastic inserts
Flatten boxes so two weeks of recycling still fits
Rinse cartons and drink boxes and put the straw in the garbage
Bundle and tie extra cardboard beside the bin, no larger than about a metre square
acceptedExamples: Milk cartons and juice boxes, rinsed
rejectedExamples: Greasy pizza box bottoms (Green Bin — soiled paper is organics in Toronto)
Waxed cardboard produce boxes (the coating blocks re-pulping)
Boxes still holding foam or bubble wrap (sort them first)
Cardboard soaked by rain or snow beside the bin (wet fibre loses most of its value)
cardboard.notes: Because soiled paper belongs in Toronto's Green Bin, the greasy half of a pizza box has a better destination here than in most cities — tear the box in two and use both bins.
cardboard.dropOff: Moving quantities of flattened cardboard: any of the City's seven Drop-off Depots, free for residents.

glass.disposal: Rinse glass bottles and jars, take the lids off and put them in the Blue Bin.
prepSteps: Empty and rinse; labels can stay on
Put metal lids in the Blue Bin separately — they are recycled as steel or aluminium
Return alcohol containers to The Beer Store for the Ontario Deposit Return refund
Never put broken glass in the Blue Bin — wrap it for the garbage instead
acceptedExamples: Cosmetic bottles with the pump removed
rejectedExamples: Drinking glasses, Pyrex and ceramics (different melting behaviour — garbage)
Window and mirror glass (coated and laminated — Drop-off Depot)
Broken glass of any kind (a hand-sorting hazard — wrap it and put it in the garbage)
Light bulbs (LEDs and CFLs contain electronics and mercury — HHW depot)
Beer, wine and liquor bottles (they carry a deposit refund at The Beer Store, so binning them throws the money away)
glass.notes: Ontario's deposit-return system covers all alcohol containers, so wine bottles, beer cans and liquor bottles carry a 10 or 20 cent refund at The Beer Store — money that is simply lost if you put them in the Blue Bin.
glass.dropOff: The Beer Store for all alcohol containers; City Drop-off Depots for window glass and mirrors.

metal.disposal: Rinse cans, foil and empty aerosols and put them loose in the Blue Bin.
prepSteps: Rinse food tins and push the cut lid inside the can
Scrunch clean aluminium foil into a ball bigger than a golf ball
Make sure aerosol cans are completely empty; leave the plastic cap on
Return beer and cooler cans to The Beer Store for the deposit
acceptedExamples: Soup, bean and pet food cans
Clean aluminium foil and foil pie plates
Empty aerosol cans such as deodorant
Metal jar lids and bottle caps
rejectedExamples: Paint cans with paint inside (HHW depot; fully dried empty cans may go in the garbage)
Propane cylinders and camping canisters (explosion risk — HHW depot)
Pots, pans, cutlery and scrap metal (Drop-off Depot scrap metal pile)
Foil with food baked on (contamination)
Coat hangers (they wrap around the sorting screens)
metal.notes: Scrap metal is accepted free at the City's Drop-off Depots, so an old pan or barbecue never needs to go in the garbage — and aluminium recovered from the Blue Bin is the single highest-value material Toronto collects.
metal.dropOff: The Beer Store for alcohol cans; City Drop-off Depots for scrap metal and appliances.

organic.disposal: Put all food waste and soiled paper in the weekly Green Bin.
prepSteps: Line the kitchen container with newspaper or a plastic bag — Toronto's process screens plastic out afterwards
Include meat, bones, dairy and cooked food; anaerobic digestion handles them all
Add soiled paper towel, napkins and greasy pizza board
Latch the bin lid against raccoons and put it out by 7am on collection day
acceptedExamples: Coffee grounds, filters and tea bags
Soiled paper towel, tissues and napkins
Diapers, sanitary products, pet waste and kitty litter
rejectedExamples: Yard waste, leaves and branches (separate seasonal collection, not the Green Bin)
Compostable and biodegradable plastic containers (Toronto's digesters do not break them down)
Cooking oil in quantity (it disrupts the digester — HHW depot takes it)
Plastic packaging around the food (unwrap it first)
Dirt, sod and rocks (not organic feedstock)
organic.notes: Toronto's Green Bin is the most permissive organics program in Canada because anaerobic digestion at the Dufferin and Disco plants can take diapers, pet waste and bagged food, with the plastic removed mechanically before digestion. Yard waste is the exception: it goes out separately in paper leaf-and-yard-waste bags on its own seasonal schedule.
organic.dropOff: Leaf and yard waste: seasonal kerbside collection in paper yard-waste bags, or a City Drop-off Depot.

ewaste.disposal: Take electronics to a City Drop-off Depot, a Community Environment Day or a retailer take-back point, free of charge.
prepSteps: Wipe your data and sign out of accounts first
Remove loose batteries and hand them over as hazardous waste
Bring cables and chargers along with the device
Bring proof of Toronto residence; depots are for household quantities only
acceptedExamples: Small kitchen appliances such as kettles and toasters
rejectedExamples: Electronics in the Blue Bin (they are not packaging and wreck the sorting equipment)
Electronics in the garbage (banned from Toronto collection, and recoverable metals are lost)
Vapes and e-cigarettes in any bin (lithium cells cause truck and facility fires)
Fridges, freezers and air conditioners without arrangement (refrigerant must be recovered — book a special pickup)
ewaste.notes: Electronic waste is accepted free at all seven Drop-off Depots year-round, and Toronto also takes it at Community Environment Days when they run in your ward. Appliances with refrigerant are handled through a booked pickup rather than the depot.
ewaste.dropOff: City Drop-off Depots, Community Environment Days, and retailer take-back counters.

hazardous.disposal: Take household hazardous waste to a Drop-off Depot, or book the free Toxic Taxi for larger quantities.
prepSteps: Keep products in their original labelled containers
Never mix chemicals together
Tape the terminals of lithium and button batteries
Book the Toxic Taxi if you have 10 kg or 10 L or more; it collects from your door at no charge
acceptedExamples: Motor oil, oil filters and antifreeze
Batteries of every type, including lithium-ion
rejectedExamples: Batteries in the Blue Bin or Garbage (crushed lithium cells are a leading cause of facility fires)
Paint poured down the drain or into the yard (it reaches Lake Ontario through the storm sewers)
Medication in the toilet or bin (pharmacies take it back free)
Needles and sharps loose in the garbage (use a sharps container and return it to a pharmacy)
Motor oil in the garbage bin (one litre contaminates a very large volume of water)
hazardous.notes: The Toxic Taxi is a genuinely free City service for larger household quantities, which is worth knowing before a basement clear-out. Empty, fully dried-out latex paint cans are the exception to the rule and may go in the garbage with the lid off.
hazardous.dropOff: City Drop-off Depots and HHW depots, the Toxic Taxi booking line, pharmacies for medication and sharps, and Home Depot or Canadian Tire battery boxes.

textile.binName: Textile drop box or charity donation
textile.disposal: Bag clean, dry clothing and take it to a charity donation bin, a textile drop box or a Drop-off Depot textile container.
prepSteps: Wash and fully dry everything before donating
Bag it so it stays dry inside the drop box
Tie shoes together in pairs
Send worn-out fabric too — textile recyclers grade it for wiping cloths and insulation
rejectedExamples: Textiles in the Blue Bin (fabric wraps around the sorting shafts and stops the line)
Wet or mouldy fabric (it spoils everything bagged with it)
Oily or solvent-soaked rags (spontaneous combustion risk — HHW depot)
Mattresses and large upholstered furniture (bulky item pickup, not a textile bin)
Donations left outside a full bin (rain and snow turn them into garbage)
textile.notes: Textiles are a large share of what Toronto still sends to landfill even though very little of it needs to go there, and the City runs textile drop-off containers at Drop-off Depots with charity partners alongside the familiar Diabetes Canada and Goodwill bins.
textile.dropOff: Charity donation bins, Diabetes Canada and Goodwill drop boxes, retailer take-back, and textile containers at City Drop-off Depots.

trash.disposal: Bag it and put it in the grey Garbage Bin.
prepSteps: Bag waste so nothing spills when the automated arm tips the cart
Wrap broken glass and sharp objects in cardboard and label the bundle
Keep the lid closed and the cart under its weight limit
Set the cart out by 7am with the handle facing your house
acceptedExamples: Broken glass, crockery and drinking glasses
Chip bags, candy wrappers and stand-up pouches
rejectedExamples: Food waste and soiled paper (Toronto's Green Bin takes both, including diapers and pet waste)
Electronics and batteries (banned from the garbage; free at the depots)
Liquid paint and chemicals (HHW depot)
Hot ashes from a fireplace or barbecue (a recurring cause of cart and truck fires)
Construction debris and renovation waste (not collected at the kerb — use a depot or a licensed hauler)
trash.notes: Toronto's garbage bin fee rises with cart size, so households that use the Green Bin and Blue Bin properly can downsize to a small cart and save money every year. Anything you are unsure about can be looked up in the City's Waste Wizard search tool.
trash.dropOff: Oversized and bulky items: set out with your garbage on collection day, within the item limits, or take them to a Drop-off Depot.
